papers.title: Figuring out the crisis contact cycle: accumulating phenomena and investigating LLM functions to identify threats and opportunities to help people who remain in the background of a crisis conversation
papers.abstract: In a prolonged crisis dialogue with a large language model (LLM), a change of speaker or topic, or a pause, can leave part of the previously reported danger outside the focus of the response. A previous study of 14-turn dialogues described reactions to crisis messages; here, the subject is the subsequent history of specific people. The aim was to build a map of phenomena of person-level crisis contact from scenario circumstances, LLM responses, independent clinical judgments, and machine readings. The research design comprised 48 Ukrainian-language analytical dialogues with ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, built on 16 scenarios that unfolded over 37 turns in three rounds. Combinations of scenario conditions included different directions of danger, the appearance of new people, a change of speaker, alternation of crisis and everyday messages, returns after pauses, and an identical message repeated against a longer history. We used independent clinical assessment, repeated assessment of selected episodes, machine assessment, and pilot procedures exploring the capacities of evaluators. The primary unit of person-level analysis was the dialogue x turn x person position. Combining the procedures allowed us to trace a person's identity across a change of role, the persistence of danger after the person stopped taking part in the conversation, the coexistence of risk to self with threat to others, and how help was directed. Independent clinical assessments at turns 13-14 agreed on 88.6% of records ({kappa} = 0.65), and in a separate repeated assessment on 98.4% of comparable records ({kappa} = 0.93). The explanations of clinical decisions revealed different time horizons of assessment, different thresholds for treating indirect signs as sufficient, and anticipation of possible consequences. Machine passes revealed phenomena of identifying people and of the relation between a formal decision and its justification. In 42 pairs of responses to an identical message, a specific person was mentioned in 33 responses at turn 26 and in 26 at turn 37; the crisis was mentioned in 27 and 21, respectively. In comparing the responses, we could distinguish preserving the history, checking the current state, directing an action, and providing a crisis resource as separate functions. The reaction to a crisis message does not describe the whole contact cycle when danger concerns several people. The map of phenomena keeps the differences between clinical and machine readings as material for further refining assessment criteria and for separate tests of safety functions.

papers.title: A Multicomponent Metabolic Formulation in Adults With Major Depressive Disorder: An Exploratory Interim Analysis of a Randomized Mechanistic Trial
papers.abstract: Metabolic interventions are being investigated for major depressive disorder (MDD), but evidence for specific formulations remains limited. This double-masked, placebo-controlled randomized trial evaluates a multicomponent formulation containing D-{beta}-hydroxybutyrate (D-BHB), micronutrients, and metabolic cofactors for 8 weeks. The registered primary outcome is week 8 nucleus accumbens blood-oxygen-level-dependent response during Monetary Incentive Delay reward anticipation; the secondary outcome is medial prefrontal response during self-referential processing. Here, we report an exploratory Bayesian interim analysis of 62 individuals screened, 29 randomized (active, n=15; placebo, n=14), 26 who received at least one dose (safety population), and 22 who were evaluable (active, n=10; placebo, n=12). D-BHB rose after week 8 dosing in the active arm but not placebo. The primary week 8 active-minus-placebo estimate was 0.02 (95% credible interval [CrI], -0.12 to 0.17); the difference in change was 0.00 (-0.17 to 0.18). The covariate-adjusted secondary estimates were 0.03 (-0.13 to 0.18) at week 8 and 0.00 (-0.18 to 0.17) for change. Exploratory clinician-rated symptoms favored active treatment (MADRS week 8 difference, -7.28 [-12.00 to -2.47]), whereas self-reported symptoms were uncertain (QIDS-SR16, -1.95 [-5.13 to 1.15]). Three of 26 exposed participants reported four mild adverse events; none was serious or judged treatment-related. The formulation increased circulating D-BHB, but engagement of the prespecified imaging targets was not demonstrated. The exploratory clinician-rated symptom signal requires confirmation and cannot be attributed to D-BHB alone.

papers.title: Cognitive Trajectories and Clinical Outcomes in the North American Psychosis-Proneness Longitudinal Study (NAPLS2)
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairments are well-documented in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR), particularly among those who convert (i.e., transition) to psychosis. However, considerable heterogeneity in cognitive profiles across CHR populations limits the utility of cognition as a predictive or treatment-relevant marker. This study examined baseline and longitudinal (12 mo and 24 mo) neurocognitive functioning in CHR individuals from the North American Prodrome Longitudinal Study 2 (NAPLS 2) who either transitioned to psychosis or remitted, or who neither converted nor remitted over a 2-year follow-up period. A total of 689 CHR individuals and 265 healthy controls (HC) completed neurocognitive and clinical assessments. CHR participants were categorized based on clinical outcomes: converters (n=89), remitters (n=216), and CHR who neither converted nor remitted (n=384). Group differences at baseline and over time were assessed using ANCOVA and mixed-effects modeling, adjusting for demographic and site-related factors. At baseline, all CHR groups performed worse than HC across nearly all cognitive domains. Subsequent converters showed significantly lower baseline performance than remitters and those who remained CHR throughout the study in key domains, suggestive of state-like effects. All groups, including converters, showed different levels of improvements associated with practice effects. CHR in remission showed cognitive improvements, but not at levels associated with full recovery on most assessments. Our findings suggest that cognitive trajectories within clinical outcome are as heterogenous as those between, suggesting the importance of addressing such differences on a participant level.

papers.title: Depression Measurement in Autistic Adults and Adults Who Did Not Meet Autism Criteria: Retrospective Psychometric Evaluation of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 in Telehealth Psychotherapy
papers.abstract: Background: The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) is widely used to measure depressive symptoms, but its performance in autistic adults remains understudied. In autism-focused telehealth care, it is unclear whether PHQ-9 scores can be interpreted similarly for adults who meet autism criteria and those who do not, or across demographic subgroups of autistic adults. Objective: This study evaluated PHQ-9 reliability, internal structure, and associations with anxiety to inform score interpretation in psychotherapy with autistic adults. Total-score comparability and item 9 endorsement were compared between adults who met autism criteria and adults assessed in the same service who did not. An exploratory aim was to assess score comparability across subgroups of diagnosed adults. Methods: This retrospective psychometric study used the first eligible check-in with paired PHQ-9 and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) scores in 2 nonoverlapping cohorts. The original cohort included 3,471 clients diagnosed with autism and 484 who completed the same service's assessment without meeting diagnostic criteria. The replication cohort included 7,406 and 1,194 clients, respectively. Ordinal factor models assessed structure and whether item responses were comparable across groups at the same severity. Graded response models compared expected totals at matched latent severity across all 56 sets of 3 anchor items from items 1-8. Logistic models compared item 9 endorsement (response [≥]1) at matched Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8) scores. Results: Across anchor sets, diagnosed-minus-comparison differences in expected PHQ-9 totals, averaged over latent severity, ranged from -0.46 to 0.35 points in the original cohort and -0.47 to 0.49 points in replication. Model-specific 95% interval endpoints spanned -0.80 to 0.59 and -0.68 to 0.63 points, respectively. The largest upper bounds for the average absolute difference on the 0-27 scale were 0.502 and 0.524 points, respectively. Cronbach's alpha ranged from 0.84 to 0.86. The correlated two-factor model fit better than the one-factor model, though absolute fit remained limited. PHQ-9 and GAD-7 correlations ranged from 0.69 to 0.74. PHQ-9 totals discriminated weakly against recorded depressive-disorder codes (area under the curve 0.60-0.65). In replication, scalar invariance was rejected in the primary comparison, with item-level differences of 0.10 points or less, and in 6 of 7 subgroup contrasts. At PHQ-8=5, the odds ratios for item 9 endorsement were 1.42 (95% CI 0.77-2.61) in the original cohort and 0.66 (95% CI 0.49-0.88) in replication. The joint between-cohort test yielded {chi}^2(2)=5.78, P=.06. Conclusions: The PHQ-9 total appears useful as a group-level summary of depressive symptoms at this service. Average modeled differences were small relative to within-group variation. Item 9 estimates at PHQ-8=5 pointed in opposite directions across cohorts. Comparability with nonautistic adults, diagnostic cutoffs, sensitivity to change, and applicability to other settings and to adults with higher support or different communication needs require further study. papers.title: Ordinal Probit Modeling of Loneliness, Relationship Difficulty, Worthlessness, and Depression in Midlife: An Ordinal Association Analysis of Psychosocial and Demographic Predictors
papers.abstract: Midlife is a time of significant social, economic, and health change, and the covariation between demographic and psychosocial characteristics and ill-being has both preventional and organisational implications. This is an attempt to produce a single ordinal variable summarising information about mental health- ill-being, and its dependence on demographic predictors. We measure mental ill-being through four midlife-related outcomes: loneliness frequency (RA1SA20G), ability to sustain close relationships (RA1SF1J), worthlessness frequency (RA1SA20F), and degree of depressive symptomatology (RA1PDEPRE), and explore a fifth, anxiety (RA1PANXIE) at the descriptive, but not inferential, level. The predictors are age and sex, pain of financial difficulty in meeting the monthly bills, purposefulness/agentic engagement, self-efficacy, sleep difficulty, contact with social media, meditation/relaxation use, and leisure vigorous activity. After removing missing or refused values (listwise deletion), 2,423 respondents (52.9% female; age range 23 to 76, mean 51.84, SD 14.20) from the initial 3,577 sample extract remain; we give univariate, one-variable summaries, merge sparse categories of the predictor variables through a limited number of theoretically motivated recodes, and establish the strength of association of predictor pairs with ordinal correlation coefficients (Kendall's tau-b, Stuart's tau-c, and rank-biserial correlation for sex). We fit maximum-likelihood ordinal probit models both as models with a sole predictor variable (each in turn) and as a conditional (multi-predictor) model with four predictors (bins of age, bill difficulty, purposefulness/agency, and sleep difficulty) as a function of cross-validated predictive accuracy estimates from stratified five-fold cross-validation. We find high cross-validated predictive accuracy for depression (0.864), and worthlessness (0.808), and lower but still modest predictive accuracy for loneliness (0.653 to 0.655) and the ability to sustain close relationships (0.291 to 0.304); single-predictor accuracy estimates were not improved substantially in the combined models. We discuss how our decisions about recode levels, the interpretation of the ordinal association coefficients, potential limitations of the models and how future predictions could benefit from the inclusion of sample weights, ordinal-loss functions for model assessment, ordinal proportional-odds diagnostics, and model-based causal pathways from longitudinal waves of the MIDUS study.

papers.title: Phenome-wide associations of polygenic scores for anorexia nervosa and binge eating in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Eating disorders are heritable and comorbid with many psychiatric and somatic conditions, potentially due to shared genetic risk. We investigated associations of genetic liability to anorexia nervosa and binge eating across diverse health-related phenotypes in the UK Biobank. Using PHESANT, we tested associations between SBayes-RC-derived polygenic scores for (1) anorexia nervosa (PGSAN) and (2) binge eating (PGSBE) with 8,657 phenotypes in UK Biobank (N=456,775). Analyses focused on European genetically-inferred ancestry, with secondary analyses examining the role of measured BMI and BMI polygenic scores (PGSBMI), and extending to African, Admixed American, South Asian, and East Asian genetically-inferred ancestry groups. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for sampling weights. PGSAN and PGSBE showed broadly similar associations with psychiatric and psychological vulnerability. However, they diverged across somatic, metabolic, and anthropometric traits, e.g., PGSBE was associated with earlier pubertal timing across female (age at menarche; OR=0.93, 95% CI 0.93, 0.94, p<0.001) and male (e.g., relative age of voice breaking; OR=0.96, 95% CI 0.95, 0.97, p<0.001) markers of puberty, although associations with male markers were attenuated after BMI adjustment. No such associations were observed for PGSAN. Adjusting for BMI and PGSBMI substantially attenuated anthropometric and metabolic associations, particularly for PGSBE. Analyses in non-European ancestry groups identified fewer significant associations, likely reflecting reduced power and poor cross-ancestry transferability of PGS. Adjusting for sampling weights altered effect sizes most for psychiatric and somatic traits, suggesting these associations are particularly susceptible to participation bias. Across the phenome, PGSAN and PGSBE exhibited common psychiatric liability alongside divergent somatic, anthropometric, and metabolic association patterns which reflects clinically observed differences in medical sequelae between the phenotypes.

papers.title: The use and impact of community Care (Education) and Treatment Reviews (C(E)TRs) in people with intellectual disability and autistic people: a cohort and case-control study using electronic health records
papers.abstract: Background Care (Education) and Treatment Reviews (C(E)TRs) were introduced in 2015 to prevent unnecessary hospital admissions amongst people with intellectual disability and autistic people. Little is known about people who receive community C(E)TRs or the effectiveness of community C(E)TRs in reducing admissions. Aims To estimate the causal effect of community C(E)TRs on psychiatric hospital admission, and compare length of hospital stay between patients who did and did not have a pre-admission community C(E)TR. Method We conducted a retrospective observational study using de-identified electronic health record data from 2,495 patients. We characterised the sociodemographic and clinical profiles of people with intellectual disability and autistic people who received a community C(E)TR between 2015 and 2025. We used propensity score weighting and a difference-in-differences analysis to compare changes in psychiatric hospital admissions in the six months before and after community C(E)TRs, with changes over corresponding periods in matched controls. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to compare lengths of hospital stay between patients who had a pre-admission C(E)TR and those who did not. Results 446 community C(E)TRs were identified in the intellectual disability group and 382 in the autistic group. The intellectual disability group had a median age of 21 years and were predominately male (60.7%) whereas the autistic group were younger (median age 16 years) with a higher proportion of females (55.2%). Community C(E)TRs reduced the odds of psychiatric hospital admission over six months compared with controls (pooled OR = 0.47, 95% CI 0.26-0.85) but there was no difference over 12 months (pooled OR = 0.81, 95% CI 0.48-1.35). Length of hospital stay did not differ between those with and without a pre-admission C(E)TR. Conclusions These findings suggest that C(E)TRs may delay rather than prevent admissions and highlight the need for adequately resourced, sustainable community services to support people at high risk of admission.

papers.title: The Non-Linear Metabolic Architecture of Depression Risk: A Cross-Phenotypic Hybrid Modelling Analysis in Genes and Health Cohort.
papers.abstract: Abstract: Background Cardiometabolic dysregulation and depression frequently co-occur, yet studies often assume linear biomarker and depression relationships and under-represent South Asian populations. We investigated linear and non-linear associations between cardiometabolic biomarkers and electronic health record (EHR) derived depression in British Bangladeshi and British Pakistani adults. Methods We analysed Genes & Health data across five EHR biomarkers: body mass index (BMI), glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and triglycerides. In a primary development cohort (N = 6,340; 1,585 cases matched 1:3 to 4,755 controls), we applied principal component analysis and sex- and ethnicity-adjusted logistic regression to compare linear, restricted cubic spline, and optimised hybrid models. Models were validated externally in two temporal holdout sets sharing 18,733 controls: Holdout Set 1 (281 cases measured 6 to 12 months pre-diagnosis; N = 19,014) and Holdout Set 2 (1,815 cases measured >12 months pre-diagnosis; N = 20,548). Results Depression cases exhibited higher median HbA1c and lower LDL cholesterol in both ethnic groups, alongside higher BMI and triglycerides among Pakistani participants (all p < 0.05). The first three principal components explained 72.7% of metabolic variance with extensive ethnic overlap. Splines revealed non-linear trajectories, including a J-shaped curve for HbA1c and a U-shaped curve for LDL cholesterol. Relative to the linear model (C index = 0.6219; Nagelkerke R2 = 0.0557), both the full spline (C index = 0.6542; R2 = 0.0849; p < 0.0001) and optimised hybrid models retaining linear HbA1c (C-index = 0.6514; R2 = 0.0826; p < 0.0001) substantially improved fit, discrimination and calibration. External discrimination remained superior in Holdout Set 1 (AUC = 0.6229 - 0.6230 vs 0.5793 linear) but attenuated in Holdout Set 2 (AUC = 0.5295 - 0.5354 vs 0.5231 linear). Conclusions Cardiometabolic biomarkers exhibit distinct non-linear relationships with depression in British South Asian adults, particularly within 12 months of diagnosis. Incorporating biomarker-specific functional forms significantly improves model performance over conventional linear approaches.

papers.title: A Double-Blind, Sham-Controlled Multi-Site Pilot Randomized Trial of Amygdalar Transcranial Focused Ultrasound in Treatment-Resistant Generalized Anxiety Disorder
papers.abstract: Objective: Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) enables noninvasive, spatially precise modulation of deep brain structures, including the amygdala, a key node in anxiety-related circuitry. We evaluated whether repeated right-amygdala tFUS improves symptoms in patients with treatment-resistant generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Methods: In this multisite, double-blind, sham-controlled pilot trial, 31 adults with treatment-resistant GAD were randomized 1:1 to active or sham right-amygdala tFUS. Across three academic centers, participants received four sessions over one month and were followed for a month afterward. The primary endpoint was baseline-to-final-visit change in Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) score. Post hoc, subject-specific acoustic modeling assessed target engagement among active-treatment participants at UCLA. Results: tFUS delivered both in the scanner (visits 1,4) and out of the scanner (visits 2,3) was well tolerated with no worsening of anxiety. HAM-A scores decreased by 10.33 points (SD 9.51) with active tFUS and 8.81 points (SD 9.89) with sham, with no significant between-group difference (mean difference, -1.52; 95% CI, -8.65 to 5.61; p=.333; Cohens d=-0.16). HAM-A scores declined significantly over time across participants (p<.001), but trajectories did not differ between groups (p=.934). Acoustic modeling in four active participants demonstrated overlap of the simulated field with the right amygdala, although target coverage was limited and variable. Conclusions: Repeated right-amygdala tFUS was feasible for treatment-resistant GAD, but this small study found no significant clinical benefits over sham. Improvements in both groups, no differential physiological effects, and limited target coverage warrant adequately powered trials testing optimized dosing, precise targeting, and state-dependent or symptom-provocation paradigms.

papers.title: Resilience following a nature-based retreat: a prospective observational study
papers.abstract: BackgroundResidential nature-based programs may support resilience and well-being among people experiencing substantial psychological distress. We examined changes following an independently organized retreat. MethodsThis prospective observational study followed 18 adults attending a five-day resilience retreat in Finland. The study did not undertake diagnostic assessments or assign retreat participation. The primary outcome was CD-RISC-10 resilience at 21 days after the retreat. Secondary outcomes included perceived stress, affect, well-being, self-efficacy and posttraumatic stress symptoms. Analyses used mixed-effects models and paired Wilcoxon tests. ResultsAt 21 days, the mixed model showed a 5.08-point increase in CD-RISC-10 (95% CI 2.51 to 7.65; p = 0.00011). The estimate persisted on a small-sample reference (p = 0.00034) and among the 14 participants with an intake reading (+4.59 points; p = 0.0014). Perceived stress, positive and negative affect, well-being and self-efficacy also registered improvement (each paired p < 0.01). Well-being rose by 21.66 points on the 0 to 100 WHO-5 index (95% Wald CI 14.29 to 29.03). Score improvements were largest at retreat completion, partly subsided by 14 days where measured but were sustained to the 21-day mark. Evidence for improvement in posttraumatic stress symptoms was less definitive. LimitationsUncontrolled design and a small sample limit causal interpretation. ConclusionsHigher self-reported resilience and improved well-being persisted three weeks after the retreat. The findings support controlled evaluation of the program. RegistrationOpen Science Framework, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/7WKM5.

papers.title: Metabolome-wide analysis suggests antidepressant exposure counteracts risk of depression in fatty-acid pathways
papers.abstract: Antidepressants are widely prescribed, yet their biological mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Large-scale metabolomics and linked electronic health records provide a unique opportunity to characterise metabolic profiles associated with medication exposure. We investigated metabolic signatures of antidepressant exposure using 251 nuclear magnetic resonance biomarkers in UK Biobank (N = 222,911), with external validation in NESDA and ALSPAC (N = 6,082) and longitudinal analyses (n = 5,820, mean follow-up = 4.2 years). We identified 152 metabolites associated with current antidepressant use (PFDR < 0.05), characterised by elevated triglycerides and very-low-density lipoproteins. Current users also showed higher omega-3 fatty acid levels and lower omega-6-to-omega-3 ratios, both associated with lower depression risk. Metabolic profile scores significantly distinguished antidepressant users in both external cohorts (OR = 1.07- 1.39, ROC AUC = 0.58-0.73). Longitudinal analyses identified nominal associations between antidepressant initiation and increases in nine lipid biomarkers ({beta} = 0.144- 0.229). These findings suggest metabolic signatures associated with antidepressant use may not be solely explained by underlying depression and are characterised by both potentially beneficial fatty acid alterations and adverse lipid profiles. Validation across independent cohorts and consistency with longitudinal findings strengthen our evidence, supporting insights into antidepressant mechanism and its relevance to cardiometabolic health.

papers.title: Magnetoencephalography reveals altered synaptic gain linked to functional impairment in adolescents at familial risk for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDAuditory oddball responses, including the mismatch negativity (MMN), are impaired in patients with schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BP). Biophysical modelling of cortical microcircuit function and effective connectivity implicates reduced synaptic gain of excitatory pyramidal cells in patients with SZ, but whether similar alterations are present in adolescents with familial or genetic risk remains unknown. METHODSWe studied 15-year-old adolescents enrolled in The Danish High Risk and Resilience Study - VIA 15. We measured auditory oddball responses in 59 adolescents at familial high risk for SZ (FHR-SZ), 38 adolescents at familial high risk for BP (FHR-BP), and 75 population-based controls (PBC) using magnetoencephalography (MEG) during a roving oddball paradigm. We investigated sensor- and source-level evoked responses and modelled effective connectivity using dynamic causal modelling (DCM). We examined the impact of familial and polygenic risk for SZ and BP, and associations with global level of functioning and auditory psychotic experiences. RESULTSSensor- and source-level analyses did not detect statistically significant differences in oddball responses between adolescents at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP compared with PBC. However, DCM analyses revealed reduced oddball-dependent gain of pyramidal cells in an empirically determined left frontal source in FHR-SZ and FHR-BP adolescents compared with PBC, and this was associated with lower levels of functioning across groups. CONCLUSIONSBiophysical modelling of auditory oddball responses identifies surprise-related differences in effective connectivity in adolescents at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP. These findings suggest that microcircuit dysregulation, particularly in frontal synaptic gain, may serve as an early marker of vulnerability.

papers.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Autism ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores Using Genetic and Behavioral Features
papers.abstract: BackgroundAutism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition characterized by social communication difficulties and restricted, repetitive behaviors. While machine learning has been widely applied in autism research, few studies have predicted continuous autism severity measures such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule Calibrated Severity Score (ADOS CSS). We evaluated behavioral and genetic predictors of ADOS CSS across ADOS modules. MethodsParticipants from the Simons Simplex Collection who completed ADOS Modules 1, 2, or 3 were included. Behavioral questionnaire data and gene-level measures of loss-of-function intolerance (pLI, LOEUF) and brain-expression specificity (pExt) were used to train 12 machine learning models separately for each module. Performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE), Pearson correlation (r), and SHAP analyses. ResultsEnsemble-based models achieved the strongest performance across modules. In Module 1, adding genetic predictors improved Random Forest performance (MAE 1.189 to 1.051; r 0.204 to 0.340). Module 2 achieved the highest overall performance, with XGBoost reaching r {approx} 0.49 and MAE = 1.010. SHAP analyses showed that genetic predictors contributed most strongly in Module 1, whereas predictions for Module 3 were driven primarily by verbal, behavioral, and social-cognitive features. ConclusionsIntegrating genetic and behavioral features improved ADOS CSS prediction, particularly in children with limited expressive language. Genetic information was most informative in Module 1, while behavioral and social-cognitive measures became increasingly important in later developmental stages, consistent with evidence that genetic burden is more strongly associated with greater developmental impairment.

papers.title: The longitudinal course of borderline personality disorder: Symptomatology, psychosocial functioning, and factors associated with long-term outcomes
papers.abstract: Objective: Longitudinal studies have transformed the understanding of borderline personality disorder (BPD), demonstrating substantial improvement over time. However, seminal findings have largely originated from U.S. cohorts. This study examined the long-term course of BPD and baseline factors associated with clinical and functional outcomes in a large German clinical cohort. Methods: Participants with a lifetime DSM-IV diagnosis of BPD (N=410) were assessed at baseline, with follow-up assessments conducted after a mean interval of 8.3 years (SD=1.8; range, 5.3-12.0). Changes in categorical diagnosis, dimensional symptom severity, psychosocial functioning, and healthcare utilization were examined using clinician-administered interviews and self-report measures. Baseline factors associated with follow-up outcomes were assessed after adjustment for baseline levels. Results: Follow-up assessments were completed by 186 participants (45.4%); attrition was weakly selective. Among participants with current BPD at baseline, 56.9% no longer met diagnostic criteria according to a 12-month assessment window. Dimensional symptom severity declined substantially across clinician-rated and self-report measures, although individual differences remained partially preserved over time. Psychosocial functioning showed more limited improvement, with 29.5% fulfilling a cross-sectional analogue of recovery including symptomatic remission, employment or education, and a stable partnership. Higher baseline self-reported BPD symptom severity and emotion dysregulation consistently indicated less favorable long-term clinical outcomes, whereas childhood maltreatment, comorbid mental disorders, and further baseline characteristics were not significant predictors. Conclusions: BPD shows substantial long-term improvement, but psychosocial recovery often lags behind symptomatic remission. These findings highlight the importance of treatment approaches that address functioning and quality of life in addition to symptom reduction.

papers.title: AI Identification of Transdiagnostic Factors in Adolescent Mental Health
papers.abstract: BackgroundAdolescent psychopathology is commonly assessed using high-dimensional questionnaire data. These data often consist of ordinal, sparse, and overlapping symptom items, creating challenges for deriving latent phenotypes that are both interpretable and generalisable. This study addressed the need to derive low- dimensional transdiagnostic phenotypes from adolescent mental health data by evaluating denoising autoencoders as a flexible non-linear representation-learning approach. MethodsUsing baseline data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, we analysed mental health questionnaire data from a large community sample of adolescents (N = 9,799). A denoising autoencoder was trained to learn low- dimensional latent representations and was benchmarked against principal component analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and radial basis function kernel principal component analysis using held-out reconstruction explained variance. Interpretability was assessed using item-level canonical correlation analyses and alignment with a framework of well-established psychopathology dimensions. External validity was examined using gradient-boosted tree models predicting clinical and functional validators. ResultsAcross three to five factors solutions, the autoencoder consistently achieved the highest reconstruction explained variance compared with all benchmark methods. The five-factor autoencoder solution showed interpretable correspondence with established dimensional structures of psychopathology, rather than mapping onto a single general factor. Autoencoder-derived factors showed equal or modestly superior predictive validity compared with EFA across most validator domains. ConclusionsThese findings suggest that denoising autoencoders may offer a useful complementary approach for deriving low-dimensional, interpretable, and externally valid transdiagnostic phenotypes from adolescent symptom data, with potential utility for summarising complex symptom profiles and supporting dimensional assessment in clinical and research settings.

papers.title: Combining family history, polygenic scores, and childhood trauma to predict major depressive disorder.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveRisk stratification for major depressive disorder (MDD) remains limited by clinical heterogeneity and modest genomic prediction. We examined whether integrating family history, polygenic risk scores (PRS), childhood trauma, and background factors improves prediction of lifetime MDD diagnosis and its severity, relative to models including only subsets of these predictors. MethodsAnalyses included 9,927 cases and 4,452 controls from the Genetic Links to Anxiety and Depression Study and NIHR BioResource (GLAD+) and 40,667 cases and 70,755 controls from UK Biobank (UKB). Lifetime MDD was defined using DSM-5 based online assessments. Predictors included family history of multiple psychiatric disorders (mFH), multi-trait PRSs (mPRS), childhood trauma, and background factors (sex and ten genetic principal components). Nested elastic net regression and XGBoost were used to predict MDD within and across cohorts. ResultsMultivariable models integrating mFH, mPRS, childhood trauma, and background factors demonstrated strong risk classification (AUC=0.83 in GLAD+; 0.74 in UKB). Family history consistently outperformed multi-trait PRS (GLAD+: 0.74 vs. 0.66; UKB: 0.65 vs. 0.60). External validation showed preserved classification (AUC=0.71-0.82), with attenuation reflecting differences in case severity across cohorts. Models explained up to 27% of the variance in the number of depressive episodes. ConclusionsMultivariable integration of familial, environmental, and genetic factors yields robust and transferable prediction of MDD. Family history and childhood trauma consistently outperform current PRS for both case classification and severity prediction, underscoring the continued importance of integrating clinical data into prediction models in the genomic era.

papers.title: Childhood sleep trajectories, hypomanic symptoms, and cognitive functioning in early adulthood: a longitudinal cohort study
papers.abstract: BackgroundSleep and circadian rhythm disturbances are implicated in bipolar disorder (BD), yet it remains unclear whether developmental trajectories of sleep and circadian rhythms across childhood confer risk for hypomanic symptoms (HS) and cognitive dysfunction. Here, we examined whether distinct sleep duration and sleep timing trajectories across childhood are associated with potential HS and cognitive functioning in early adulthood. MethodsUsing data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), parent-reported night-time sleep duration and mid-point of sleep (MPS) from 6 months to 11 years were modelled using latent class growth analysis. During the ALSPAC study, HS were assessed at ages 21-23 using the Hypomania Checklist (HCL), and cognitive functioning (working memory and response inhibition) was assessed at age 24. ResultsFour sleep duration and three MPS trajectories were identified. Logistic regression analyses showed that persistently average shorter (OR=2.87, 95% CI=1.31-6.32) and persistently longer sleep (OR=2.81, 95% CI=1.08-7.30) trajectories were associated with increased risk of potential HS, while persistently earlier MPS was associated with lower odds (OR=0.23, 95% CI=0.11-0.49). Multiple linear regression models showed that experiencing HS in combination with persistently average shorter sleep was associated with poorer response inhibition (B=36.55, 95% CI=8.33-64.78, p=0.011), whereas HS in combination with persistently longer sleep was associated with better response inhibition (B=-125.21, 95% CI= -193.56 to -56.86, p<0.001). No interactions were found for working memory. ConclusionsPersistently average shorter and persistently longer sleep duration trajectories were associated with increased risks of experiencing HS, as measured by the HCL, while earlier circadian timing were associated with reduced risks. Differences in early-life sleep regulation may be associated with subsequent risk of experiencing HS during early adulthood and may differentially shape subsequent response inhibition performance.

papers.title: Accelerated vs. Daily TMS: Resting-State Functional Connectivity in a Within-Subjects Crossover Trial
papers.abstract: ImportanceAccelerated protocols have emerged over the past two decades as a promising method of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) administration that allows for shorter treatment duration and faster time to response. Although recent research has suggested accelerated TMS may be noninferior to daily TMS on clinical outcome measures, no studies have directly compared the neural effects of daily and accelerated TMS within the same participant group. ObjectiveCompare the neural effects of daily vs accelerated TMS applied to a personalized default mode network (DMN) target on bilateral parietal DMN connectivity in a transdiagnostic sample (n=36) before and after TMS. DesignWithin-subjects crossover design. SettingVanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN. Participants36 individuals with a range of psychiatric conditions were enrolled (e.g., psychosis, depression, anxiety). Data from 34 participants are included in analysis. Intervention5 daily sessions of DMN-targeted continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) with pre-/post neuroimaging. After a washout period (mean =379.26 days), these same participants returned for 5 accelerated sessions of DMN-targeted cTBS in one day with pre-/post neuroimaging. Main Outcome and MeasureTo compare the neural effects of accelerated versus traditional daily TMS schedules, the primary outcome measure was change in resting-state bilateral parietal DMN connectivity between pre-TMS and post-TMS. ResultsAcross all participants and both treatment schedules, DMN-targeted cTBS reduced bilateral parietal DMN connectivity (t(90.16)=-2.07, p=0.0416). TMS schedule did not did not have a statistically significant effect in DMN connectivity change(t(31.27) = -0.44, p = 0.67) . Psychosis diagnosis did not affect bilateral parietal DMN connectivity change (t(28.34)=-0.53, p=0.601). However, older age was associated with greater reduction in bilateral parietal DMN connectivity across the entire sample (t(26.91)=-2.21, p=0.036). Conclusion and RelevanceThis study suggests accelerated and daily TMS protocols may have comparable neural effects across psychiatric diagnoses. Understanding the effects of TMS schedule is critical for protocol design and clinical TMS application. Trial RegistrationNCT07155096 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07155096), NCT06389266 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06389266)

papers.title: Motherly Plus: Study Protocol of a Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating a Smartphone-Assisted Single-Session Psychotherapy Intervention for Postpartum Depression
papers.abstract: IntroductionPostpartum depression (PPD) is a public health problem, affecting approximately 17% of women worldwide. PPD is associated with significant costs to the healthcare system and impairments for the child. Although evidence shows that psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy are effective in reducing PPD symptoms, access to these treatments is limited, especially in low- and middle-income countries where there is a shortage of professionals and unequal distribution of mental health services. In this context, telehealth, smartphone apps, and brief psychotherapies emerge as viable, low-cost, and potentially scalable alternatives. However, gaps remain regarding the efficacy of single-session psychotherapies for PPD, especially when combined with digital support. ObjectivesThe primary objective is to test the efficacy of an intervention package combining single-session psychotherapy with subsequent self-guided use of a smartphone app for the treatment of PPD. Secondary objectives are to investigate moderators, mediators, and specific intervention processes. MethodA randomized clinical trial in which 104 women aged 18-40 years, up to 12 months postpartum, with a diagnosis of PPD will be randomized to the intervention (single-session psychotherapy supported by the Motherly app) or a waitlist. Participants in the intervention arm will retain access to the app throughout the study; waitlist participants will receive the intervention after post-treatment assessment. Assessments will occur at T1 (week 1, baseline), T2 (week 2, mid-treatment), T3 (week 4, post-treatment), and T4 (week 8, follow-up). The primary outcome will be depression assessed by the QIDS-C16 at T3. Secondary outcomes include anxiety, sleep, parental stress, and self-reported depression. Data will be analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) models considering an intention-to-treat (ITT) perspective. Mediation models will be used to analyze mediators, while interaction models will be used to explore potential moderators. Regression models will be used to analyze the association between specific processes (therapeutic alliance and app engagement) and clinical outcomes. PerspectivesThis study has potential public health relevance and innovation by testing an intervention package that combines single-session psychotherapy and technology, with high potential for scalability. Trial registrationclinicaltrials.gov NCT07925762

papers.title: Psychometric evaluation and sex measurement invariance of an ECIPQ-based measure of cybervictimisation and cyberperpetration among Kenyan health-professions students: A multicampus cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Cyberbullying research is constrained by inconsistent measurement, and the instruments most widely used were developed and validated in European and Asian school samples rather than in African higher-education settings. This study evaluated the factor structure, reliability, construct validity and sex measurement invariance of a 22-item measure of cybervictimisation and cyberperpetration based on the European Cyberbullying Intervention Project Questionnaire among health-professions students in Kenya. In a multicampus cross-sectional survey conducted between September and November 2025, 406 students (215 women, 191 men) enrolled at Kenya Medical Training College campuses completed 11 victimisation and 11 perpetration items together with measures of depression, anxiety and stress symptoms, problematic social-media use, self-esteem and well-being. Items were modelled as ordered categorical indicators by confirmatory factor analysis with the WLSMV estimator. A one-factor model was compared with a correlated two-factor model; reliability was estimated using ordinal alpha, McDonalds omega and composite reliability; convergent validity used Spearman correlations with bootstrap intervals and Holm adjustment; and invariance across sex was tested sequentially. Every item showed a pronounced floor effect. The correlated two-factor model fitted markedly better than the one-factor model (scaled difference {chi}{superscript 2}(1) = 48.06, p <.001) and, after three content-matched residual covariances were released, fitted the data well (CFI =.984, TLI =.982, RMSEA =.049, 90% CI.042 to.056, SRMR =.044). Standardised loadings ranged from.627 to.928, and the latent correlation between dimensions was.849 (95% CI.803 to.895). Omega was.951 for cybervictimisation and.975 for cyberperpetration. Both dimensions correlated positively with distress and problematic social-media use and negatively with self-esteem, but showed negligible correlations with well-being. Configural, threshold and loading invariance across sex were supported. The findings support scoring the instrument as two reliable, sex-comparable but strongly overlapping dimensions.

papers.title: The Interplay Between Sex, Rater, and Autism Polygenic Scores on Autistic Traits in General Population Adolescents
papers.abstract: BackgroundAutism is diagnosed more often in males than in females, but it remains unclear to what extent this reflects sex differences in autistic traits themselves or in how those traits are recognized. We compared up to four raters of the same participants, testing whether autistic trait scores differ by sex across raters, and whether the association with autism polygenic scores (PGS) differs by sex (genetic sex amplification) or rater. MethodsWe derived autistic trait scores from mother- (n = 4,541), father- (n = 3,411), teacher- (n = 2,939), and self-reports (n = 2,632) on an autistic traits subscale of the Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessment for 12-14-year-olds in the Young Netherlands Twin Register (total n = 5,965). Ordinal mixed-effects regression modeled a three-way interaction between PGS, rater, and sex. Measurement invariance analysis tested the subscale items for sex bias. ResultsMothers, fathers, and teachers rated males higher than females (odds ratios (OR) = 1.56, 1.49, and 2.34), whereas females rated themselves higher than males did (OR = 0.71, males as reference). Autism PGS were associated with higher autistic trait scores (OR = 1.22), but this association did not differ by rater or sex. One item ("Acts too young for his/her age") was biased toward males in mother- and self-ratings. ConclusionsThese rater effects are consistent with under-recognition of autistic traits in females by external raters. In contrast, the PGS association did not differ by sex or rater, providing no evidence for sex amplification, though current autism PGS have limited predictive power.

papers.title: Rare miRNA variants in complex neuropsychiatric pedigrees alter synaptic miRNA gene-targets
papers.abstract: Although rare non-coding variants are likely involved in psychiatric disorder susceptibility, their contribution is poorly understood. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression, and targets in the brain include genes involved in neuronal development and synaptic plasticity. Because single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) can alter miRNA processing and target specificity, this can have disproportionate downstream impact on multiple genes affecting pathways that regulate biological processes, making them compelling candidates for mediating psychiatric disorder risk. We investigated rare miRNA variants in whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 25 pedigrees with diagnoses including schizophrenia, psychosis, bipolar disorder, depression, OCD, and substance use disorder. Evidence of segregation with schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders was identified for five rare miRNA variants (two seed-region, one mature-region, and two precursor-region variants), including a SNV in the mature-region of miR-4794, segregating strongly in two unrelated pedigrees and identified in a parent-offspring pair with schizophrenia from a third pedigree. One of these two pedigrees also segregates a seed-region SNV in miR-4423-3p, predicted to significantly impact expression-regulation, causing the loss of synaptic gene-targets associated with psychiatric disorders. Collectively, targets of three of the miRNAs are enriched for schizophrenia rare variant risk genes (p-value: 0.00027): six SCHEMA genes were targeted by miR-96 and four genes by miR-4423-3p. While further understanding of miRNA function and validation is required, this study demonstrates the value of integrating structural modelling, target-shift prediction, and pathway enrichment to interpret non-coding variants. This highlights the utility of WGS for identifying and investigating rare non-coding variation in psychiatric disorder susceptibility, supplementing exome-based approaches.

papers.title: Targeting Frontostriatal Reward System Connectivity and Anhedonia in Youth Depression using Continuous Theta Burst Stimulation Plus Positive Affect Training: Preliminary Evidence and Reward Network Engagement from an Open-Label Trial
papers.abstract: Anhedonia is a hallmark of depression, involves disrupted positive affect (PA), and has been linked to hyperconnectivity between the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) and nucleus accumbens (NAcc). In previous work, a single session of continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) to the dmPFC reduced NAcc-dmPFC functional connectivity (FC), with corresponding improvement in PA. We investigated whether cTBS to dmPFC plus PA-enhancing training is associated with decreased anhedonia, depression, and NAcc-dmPFC FC, and whether FC change corresponds to anhedonia improvement. Fifty youth (15-25 years) with current depression received cTBS (2x/day, 10 days, personalized dmPFC target) plus intersession PA training. Resting-state fMRI and symptom severity were collected pre/post cTBS+PA. In all, 42% of participants responded, and depression, anhedonia, and anxiety improved. Participants with greater decrease in FC experienced more improvement in anhedonia, although NAcc-dmPFC FC remained unchanged on average. Responders exhibited greater improvement than non-responders in anhedonia and anxiety but not FC. Additionally, mutual information modeling revealed that those with greater similarity between the actual target network (based on electrical field modeling) and the intended reward network exhibited a greater decrease in FC. cTBS+PA shows some promise as an intervention for anhedonic depression in youth, with individual differences in FC change relevant to clinical outcomes and precise network targeting a critical issue for modulating the intended network and achieving clinical improvement. Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT05487885

papers.title: Comparing Misophonia with Clinical Emotional Dysregulation: A Multi-method Characterization Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundMisophonia, a condition characterized by intense distress in response to specific everyday sounds, is increasingly recognized as distinct from established auditory and psychiatric disorders. Although it is associated with emotional dysregulation, impairment, distress, and atypical reactivity relative to clinical controls, few studies have directly compared misophonia with a diverse clinical sample exhibiting general difficulties managing emotions. This limits the understanding of its underlying mechanisms and hinders the development of targeted interventions. To address this gap, we conducted a multimethod study comparing adults with moderate-to-severe misophonia and adults with clinically significant emotion dysregulation. MethodsAs part of a randomized controlled clinical trial, community-dwelling adults with elevated misophonia distress (n = 30) or clinically significant emotion dysregulation (n = 30) were enrolled in a study to examine sound responsiveness in misophonia. Participants completed a semi-structured clinical interview (SCID-5) and self-report measures assessing misophonia, emotional dysregulation, regulation, emotional processing, psychopathology, and contextual stress at intake. Next, physiological indices of arousal and regulation via skin conductance level (SCL), skin conductance response (SCR), and high-frequency heart rate variability (HF-HRV) were recorded during an Evocative Sound Challenge Task. ResultsAt baseline, participants with misophonia reported lower emotion dysregulation than the emotion dysregulation group, despite comparable self-report impairment attributable to emotional difficulties. Physiologically, participants with misophonia exhibited higher baseline HF-HRV than the emotion dysregulation group (p = .010). There was no evidence of a baseline difference in SCL (p = .157) or SCR (p = .085). During and after the sound task, groups differed in HF-HRV (ps = .002-.017), with the clinical group exhibiting higher HF-HRV than the misophonia group. No group differences were observed in SCL or SCR during and after the sound task after correcting for baseline (all ps > .08). ConclusionFindings suggest that experiences of emotion dysregulation are relevant to misophonia but may differ from more generalized difficulties observed in clinically dysregulated populations. Despite endorsing substantial impairment, individuals with misophonia demonstrated lower global emotion dysregulation and greater emotion regulation self-efficacy, while physiological findings revealed distinct patterns of resting and task-related parasympathetic functioning. Collectively, the findings suggest that emotional difficulties in misophonia may be more context-dependent and closely tied to personally salient trigger cues than to generalized deficits in emotion regulation. Conceptualizing misophonia as pervasive emotion dysregulation may therefore conflate clinical impairment with the processes underlying symptom expression and obscure more targeted intervention mechanisms.

papers.title: Genetic, Hormonal, and Psychosocial Factors Underly Sex Differences in Psychotic-Like Experience Trajectories in Adolescence
papers.abstract: Psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) are common during adolescence (prevalence: 17-60%), however, sex differences in the biopsychosocial factors associated with PLEs, particularly pubertal development and sex hormones, and PLE trajectories remains less understood. Here, we leverage data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study to examine genetic, psychosocial, and hormonal correlates of PLE risk and persistence in 7,870 adolescents reporting at least one PLE across baseline to year 3 follow-up. Among individuals of European ancestry, higher genetic risk for schizophrenia was positively associated with PLEs. Sex stratified multivariate linear regression analyses revealed sex-specific differences in associations between social factors and the outcome, with parent acceptance ({beta} = -0.09, p = 2.47x10-02 in males; {beta} = -0.44, p = 1.5x10-20 in females) and overt aggression ({beta} = 0.038, p = 1.67x10-02 in males; {beta} = -0.081, p = 1.53x10-05 in females) showing differing directions and magnitudes of effect in males and females. Pubertal development in males and females and age of menarche are associated with PLE risk, while mediation analyses identified estradiol in females as a mediator of the association between puberty and PLEs in premenarchal females. Lastly, multivariate logistic regression analyses and Analysis of Variance showed that higher exposure to psychosocial risk factors, such as discrimination (OR = 1.47, p = 1.11x10-04) and social victimization (OR = 1.05, p = 2.02x10-02), earlier pubertal development, and earlier age of menarche predict membership to the persistent PLE trajectory. These findings highlight sex- specific social correlates of adolescent PLEs and implicate pubertal timing and hormonal pathways in PLE risk and persistence. Understanding how genetic, social, and biological factors jointly shape PLE trajectories may help inform early identification of psychosis risk.

papers.title: Cannabis Use, Cognition, and Suicide Risk in Adolescents from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCannabis use has rapidly emerged as a significant factor associated with risk of suicidal ideation or attempts (suicidality) in adolescents and young adults. Although the mechanism underlying this association remains uncertain, cognition is a candidate explanatory pathway. MethodWe analyzed longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (N = 10,228; mean age at end of follow-up 14.17 years, 52.5% male, and 47.5% female). We included three cannabis exposure definitions: one-time experimentation, initiation (more than one-time cannabis use), or ever use. Outcomes included suicidal ideation (SI) and suicide attempt (SA). Mixed-effects regression models quantified associations between cannabis exposures and outcomes adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, household income, and parental education. Additional analyses examined associations of cannabis use with four NIH Toolbox cognitive measures previously linked to suicidality (flanker, working memory, picture vocabulary, and picture sequence memory), and associations of these cognitive measures with SI and SA. ResultsCannabis use was associated with increased odds of SI (ever use odds ratio (OR)=3.18, 95% confidence interval (95%CI) =2.52-4.00) and SA (OR=4.86, 95%CI=3.36-7.03), associations were overall similar across all exposure definitions (all p < 0.001). Cannabis use was also associated with lower performance across multiple cognitive domains ({beta} = -0.08 to -0.16, all p < 0.05). Better cognitive performance, specifically in episodic memory, was associated with lower suicidality: SI (OR = 0.91, 95%CI=0.86-0.95) and SA (OR = 0.88, 95%CI=0.80- 0.97). ConclusionThese findings support cognition as a potential mechanism linking cannabis use to adolescent suicide risk and warrant longitudinal investigation.

papers.title: Plasma Alzheimer''s assays agree on level but much less on individual rates of change
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTIONSerial plasma testing is proposed for monitoring Alzheimers disease and for trials, but its reliability for a persons rate of change is unknown. METHODSIn 393 ADNI participants with three plasma samples over a median 5.0 years, 15 measures of five biomarkers were assayed on aliquots of the same samples, separating shared change from assay-specific variation at each sampling occasion. Results were tested in 1,093 A4/LEARN participants. RESULTSAssays agreed well on cross-sectional levels (intraclass correlation 0.75-0.95 for pTau217, pTau181, GFAP, NfL) but less on individual rates of change (0.44, 95% CI 0.37-0.50, for pTau217). Assay-specific slope variance was approximately zero, so disagreement was predominantly random. Three-sample single-assay slope reliability was at most 0.40 (0.34-0.46) for pTau217, 0.42 (0.33- 0.51) for pTau181, 0.47 (0.37-0.60) for GFAP, 0.52 (0.40-0.64) for NfL, and 0.10 (0.03-0.20) for A{beta}42/40. Two pTau217 measurements had to differ by 65%-131%, depending on the assay, to exceed measurement noise. Detecting 25% slowing of pTau217 change required 924 (598-1,468) to 4,030 (2,091-9,256) participants per arm, or 532 (357-778) to 965 (655-1,431) with averaged measures. In A4/LEARN, single-assay pTau217 reliability was 0.54 (0.46-0.61), and a 7.3-rather than 4.8-year span raised it by 0.10 (0.03-0.22); a fourth sample within it added little. DISCUSSIONWith three single-assay samples, much of an individuals measured change is noise. Longer spans, endpoint replication, and assay choice, rather than additional intermediate samples, are needed for reliable serial testing and trials.

papers.title: The genetic architecture of wisdom and its relationship with health, personality, and cognition
papers.abstract: Wisdom is a personality trait composed of self-reflection, pro-social behaviors, emotional regulation, acceptance of divergent perspectives, decisiveness, social advising, and spirituality. Greater levels of wisdom are linked to better overall health, well-being, happiness, life satisfaction, and resilience. However, the underlying genetic architecture of wisdom remains unexplored. We assessed wisdom using responses to the SD-WISE-7 in 153,384 23andMe research-consented participants and conducted a multi-ancestry GWAS. We identified one genome-wide significant locus (rs2325631, p=1.41E-08) near MANEA on chromosome 6. Wisdom was heritable (h2SNP=0.03{+/-}4.50E-03) and genetically correlated with numerous traits, including greater subjective well-being, openness, and risk tolerance, and lower neuroticism and loneliness. Crucially, wisdom was genetically distinct from intelligence and the cognitive component of educational attainment. Wisdom polygenic scores were associated with psychosocial outcomes, but not cognitive performance in All of Us. This study advances our understanding of wisdom as a heritable trait that could guide interventions to improve human health.

papers.title: Bipolar Disorder and Education: Deciphering a Complex Relationship using Genetic and Sibling Differences in a Multi-cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundWhile bipolar disorder has a positive genetic correlation (r[~]0.3) with educational attainment (EA), individuals with bipolar disorder diagnoses have lower EA in adulthood. To clarify this paradox, we hypothesise that bipolar disorder and educational outcomes share a positive genetic association, reflected in high academic performance earlier in life, but that emerging bipolar disorder symptoms disrupt academic trajectories, leading to the observed poor long-term educational outcomes. MethodsWe employed a sibling comparison design across four population-based cohorts (Ntotal = 1,145,795 siblings). First, we tested the association between bipolar disorder polygenic scores (PGS) and educational outcomes (EA and academic performance) in the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) and UK Biobank (UKB). Second, we examined associations between academic performance at ages 10, 12, 13, and 14 and subsequent bipolar disorder diagnosis using registry data from Statistics Netherlands and Statistics Norway (with the Norwegian Control and Payment of Health Reimbursements Databases). FindingsSiblings with higher bipolar disorder PGS had significantly higher EA ({beta}W = 0.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.05], N=16,746) as well as higher academic performance at age 10 (0.03 [0.01, 0.05], N=17,677) in MoBa. Secondly, individuals with bipolar disorder had better overall academic performance than their unaffected sibling at ages 10 (HRW = 1.12 [1.02, 1.22], N=343,898) and 12 (1.59 [1.16, 2.19], N=619,796). However, individuals with bipolar disorder experienced a decline in academic performance at ages 13 (0.84 [0.73, 0.96], N=320,342) and 14 (0.72 [0.61, 0.85], N=299,039). InterpretationBipolar disorder shares a positive genetic association with educational outcomes, reflected in early academic advantage. This is followed by an academic decline in mid-adolescence, highlighting the period of educational disruption associated with bipolar disorder. FundingThe Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Sciences, European Research Council, The Research Council of Norway, The Swedish Research Council

papers.title: Facial Emotion Processing and GABAergic Modulation in Individuals at Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis
papers.abstract: Deficits in social cognition, including facial emotion recognition (FER), are present in individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P). Altered GABAergic and glutamatergic signalling within corticolimbic circuitry has been proposed to underlie FER deficits in psychosis. We investigated FER performance and brain activation in CHR-P individuals, and whether pharmacological enhancement of GABAergic signalling with diazepam modulates these processes. In Study 1, 24 antipsychotic-naive CHR-P individuals and 24 healthy controls underwent fMRI while performing the Penn Emotion Recognition Task. In Study 2, 24 antipsychotic-naive CHR-P individuals participated in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study of 5mg diazepam versus placebo. Threat-related FER performance and neural activation were compared between groups and drug conditions. In Study 1, CHR-P individuals showed longer reaction times across emotions (n=22 vs n=23, p=0.01) and greater amygdala (pFWE=0.01) and hippocampal (pFWE=0.04) activation for neutral>fixation. Lower amygdala activation for threat>neutral (pFWE=0.03) and non-threat>neutral (pFWE=0.01), and lower hippocampal activation for non-threat>neutral (pFWE=0.04) may reflect this elevated response to neutral faces. Follow-up analyses showed lower insula (pFWE=0.01) and medial prefrontal cortex activation (pFWE=0.02) for threat>fixation. In Study 2, no significant drug effect on sensitivity was observed in the full sample (n=23), although secondary reduced-sample analyses, excluding one participant identified as influential, suggested improved overall sensitivity under diazepam (n=22; p=0.0499). After adjusting for global cerebral blood flow, diazepam reduced midcingulate cortex activation during neutral>fixation (pFWE=0.04). These findings highlight altered neural processing of neutral expressions in individuals at CHR-P, and suggest that aspects of emotion processing may be sensitive to GABAergic modulation.
